Content:
We're used to expressing a point [MATH: P] in three-dimensional space using [MATH: (x,y,z)] (or Cartesian) coordinates. However, we can also express the coordinates of [MATH: P] differently, using a system called cylindrical polar coordinates.

Content:
In cylindrical polar coordinates, we write the position of the point as [MATH: P(r,\theta,z),] where [MATH: r] and [MATH: \theta] are the usual plane polar coordinates [MATH: (r,\theta)] and [MATH: z] is the usual Cartesian [MATH: z]-coordinate.

Graphic:

Content:
Note that

Content:
[MATH: r\geq 0, \qquad 0\leq \theta \lt 2\pi,\qquad -\infty < z < \infty.]

sections.normalized_html:
We write the position of a point in cylindrical coordinates as [MATH: (r,\theta,z),] where [MATH: r \geq 0] and [MATH: 0 \leq \theta < 2\pi.]

According to the diagram, we have the following:

  • The ray from the origin through [MATH: N'] makes an angle of [MATH: \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{\pi}{6}] radians with the positive [MATH: x]-axis.

  • The distance from the origin to [MATH: N'] is [MATH: r=\sqrt{2}.]

  • The [MATH: z]-coordinate is [MATH: z=3] because [MATH: N] lies [MATH: 3] units above the [MATH: xy]-plane.

So, the cylindrical coordinates of [MATH: N] are [MATH: \left(\sqrt{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{6}, 3\right).]

sections.normalized_html: The point [MATH: P] has cylindrical polar coordinates [MATH: \left(4, \dfrac{\pi}{6}, -8 \right).] Find the Cartesian coordinates of [MATH: P.]
sections.readable_text: The point [MATH: P] has cylindrical polar coordinates [MATH: \left(4, \dfrac{\pi}{6}, -8 \right).] Find the Cartesian coordinates of [MATH: P.]

sections.normalized_html:
If [MATH: (r, \theta, z)] are the cylindrical polar coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates [MATH: (x,y,z)] can be found by using the following formulas: [MATH: x = r\cos\theta, \qquad y = r\sin\theta, \qquad z = z.]

Calculating [MATH: x], we get

[MATH: x|= r\cos θ; = 4\cos ((π)/(6)); = 4 ⋅ (sqrt(3))/(2); = 2sqrt(3).]

Calculating [MATH: y], we get

[MATH: y|= r\sin θ; = 4\sin ((π)/(6)); = 4 ⋅ (1)/(2); = 2.]

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of [MATH: P] are [MATH: (2\sqrt3, 2, -8).]

items.title: Converting From Cartesian Coordinates to Cylindrical Polar Coordinates

sections.normalized_html: The point [MATH: A] has Cartesian coordinates [MATH: (\sqrt3,-3,\sqrt2).] What are the cylindrical polar coordinates of [MATH: A?]
sections.readable_text: The point [MATH: A] has Cartesian coordinates [MATH: (\sqrt3,-3,\sqrt2).] What are the cylindrical polar coordinates of [MATH: A?]

sections.normalized_html:
We write the position of a point in cylindrical coordinates as [MATH: (r,\theta,z),] where [MATH: r \geq 0] and [MATH: 0 \leq \theta < 2\pi.]

The Cartesian coordinates of [MATH: A] are given as [MATH: (x,y,z) = (\sqrt3,-3,\sqrt2).]

  • From these Cartesian coordinates, we know that [MATH: z=\sqrt{2}.]

  • To find the values of [MATH: r] and [MATH: \theta,] we need to find the polar coordinates of the point [MATH: (x,y) = (\sqrt 3, -3)] in the [MATH: xy]-plane.

First, we find [MATH: r,] as follows:

[MATH: r|= sqrt(x^{2} + y^{2}); = sqrt((sqrt(3))^{2} + (− 3)^{2}); = sqrt(3 + 9); = sqrt(12); = 2sqrt(3)]

Now, since [MATH: (\sqrt3,-3)] lies in the fourth quadrant, we first need to find the reference angle [MATH: \theta_R\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: θ_{R}|= \arctan|(y)/(x)|; = \arctan|(− 3)/(sqrt(3))|; = \arctan (sqrt(3)); = (π)/(3)]

Finally, we subtract the reference angle from [MATH: 2\pi\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: θ|= 2π − θ_{R}; = 2π − (π)/(3); = (5π)/(3)]

Therefore, the cylindrical coordinates of [MATH: A] are [MATH: \left(2\sqrt{3}, \dfrac{5\pi}{3}, \sqrt2 \right).]
